synopsis: ASME V&V 40 (2018) is a medical-device model-credibility standard, paired in the booklet with FDA guidance issued in November 2023; its central principle is to scale credibility evidence to model influence and decision consequence within a defined context of use [f14568, f8072, f8073, f8075]. Credibility goals should be set prospectively: there is no universal acceptance error or minimum amount of remaining physical evidence, and physical testing is retained where model risk is high or validation evidence weakest [f14622, f7790, f8076, f7834, f7835]. The booklet rates this as the most transferable reasoning framework for off-road automatic braking, but it is not proven for that application and no direct earth-moving automatic-braking equivalent was found [f8077, f8078, f7740]. Its applicability is limited to physics-based models, including vehicle dynamics and brakes; machine-learned perception requires separate assurance [f14626, f14627, f8220]. Chapter 12 recommends simulation-credibility frameworks instead of TRL for assessing the validation toolchain, while acknowledging that these frameworks can be largely declarative [f10031, f10029].

relations.note: Both identify the most transferable framework while restricting applicability to physics-based models.
Both exclude machine-learned perception and require separate assurance.
Both define model risk through model influence and decision consequence.
Both define model risk as the combination of influence and consequence.
Both tie credibility to intended use and consequences across the same frameworks.
Both state that FDA guidance builds on ASME V&V 40.
Specifies physical-data validation and eight evidence categories alongside prospective credibility goals.
Adds that changing the context of use requires new or stronger evidence.
Risk-based thresholds explain why no universal acceptance error is specified.
Adds that risk-matched credibility goals must be set in advance.
Identifies high model risk as a reason to retain physical testing.
Identifies weak validation evidence as another reason to retain physical testing.
Transferability is judged favorably despite an explicit lack of proof for off-road braking.
Clarifies the scope boundary: dynamics and brakes are covered, neural networks are not.
Identifies verification, validation and uncertainty quantification as credibility-assessment means within the context of use.
Blind-prediction gaps motivate using credibility frameworks to assess the validation toolchain.
Cross-sector practice requires physical anchors, independent validation and uncertainty evidence beyond simulator results.
Distinguishes the domains of the three ASME standards among which the booklet prioritizes V&V 40.
